name: Umar Santos

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. Everything you say stays confidential, and your name won't be attached to any of it. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I run an excavator at a big open-pit nickel mine, loading trucks and digging out the ore zones the geologists flag. For the last three months I've also been on a trial where I run a smaller excavator by remote from a cabin at the edge of the pit, with screens and joysticks. I'm still slow, honestly, and the senior operator, Hamid, can load a truck in four passes where I need six. What I like is that it's a puzzle: where to sit the machine, how to cut the face so the next shift has it easy.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: And at home, how are things?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I live with my partner Leila, she's an accountant at a firm in town. No kids yet. I've got just over a year of pay saved and some money in index funds, because I read a lot about investing. I use AI every day, for studying hydraulics, for planning my budget, even for asking why my machine's throwing a fault code. There are three other mines within an hour, so I've got options.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If it's mostly hype, that's fine. I'd still use it for small stuff.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I'm a bit disappointed, honestly, because I like the tools. At work I'd say it saves time but it's not magic. Online I'd probably post something like 'still useful, just not a revolution'.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately it means my job is safe and I keep learning. The remote trial would carry on slowly, and I'd get better on the big machine. Leila's work stays the same too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep studying hydraulics with the AI tutor, keep the remote trial going, and aim to beat Hamid's four passes within two years. Keep putting money into index funds every month. Maybe start a small side thing selling drone footage to farmers, just for fun.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. A little bored, maybe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the drone idea?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I bought a drone last year and I fly it on my days off. Farmers around here want photos of their dams and fences. Even if AI fizzles, I'd still fly my drone for the farmers on my days off, because I like having a second thing going.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Any worries left in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nickel prices go up and down a lot. If they drop, the mine might slow. But I've got savings and I could move.

The **remote trial** carries on slowly while he catches up to Hamid.

Start a small **drone footage** side business for farmers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This one's basically what I'm already living in at work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a good thing for people who learn, and I'd tell my crew to try the remote cabin. Online I'd share videos of the remote setup. With friends I'd say it's not the end of mining work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'm in a good spot because I'm already on the remote trial. Leila's the one I'd worry about, because the checking and booking work in accounting goes first. Leila (my partner) checks invoices all day at an accounting firm, and that's exactly the work the software takes first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask to go full time on the remote trial and get certified. I'd help Leila look at courses, maybe in financial advice where clients want a person. I'd keep saving and investing at the same rate.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly calm about me, but a bit uneasy for Leila.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you and Leila talk about at dinner?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Whether she should switch now or wait. I'd say switch, she'd say wait. We'd probably meet in the middle and she'd start a course.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Do you think the remote job is safe long term?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not forever. But it gives me the skills to work with whatever comes next.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. That's very fast, especially for Leila.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say publicly that this is going to need new rules, like a shorter work week or some kind of income support. At work I'd say learn the remote systems now, because that buys a few years. I'd post a lot about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd think Leila's job goes in 2028, and mine probably by 2031. The remote cabin needs fewer operators once the AI can drive the excavator alone. With AGI by 2028, Leila's accounting job goes first, and three years later the AI drives my excavator without me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd move some investments into cash and keep a year and a half of expenses ready. I'd learn robot maintenance and fleet supervision, where a person still signs off. I'd help Leila find something hands-on or people-facing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I'd be excited about the tech and scared about our income at the same time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What gets cut first if Leila's income goes?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The new car we planned and the overseas trip. We'd live on my pay and keep investing a little.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do in those three years before the robots?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Run the remote cabin, learn the robot maintenance side, and get known as the guy who knows how the system works. That's my best chance of being kept.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years for AI, eight for robots. That's manageable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we have time to set up good training and support. I'd tell my crew to start learning now. I'd share some articles online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd think I can become a robot fleet supervisor by 2034. Leila would have time to switch too. Five years of warning is enough for Leila (my partner) to change careers and for me to learn to run the robots instead of competing with them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Get certified on the remote systems, then do a fleet supervision course. Keep investing monthly. Help Leila plan a career switch within two years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but mostly hopeful.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you consider starting your own business?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe a drone survey business. It's small now, but it could grow if mines need outside contractors.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What could go wrong?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If robots supervise robots, I'm out. But I'd see that coming and change again.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. That's plenty of time for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's an opportunity if we plan well. At work I'd say the young ones should be learning robots now. Online I'd stay positive.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'm fine. Ten years of warning is the version where a junior excavator operator like me ends up running the robot fleet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep learning the remote systems, take a robotics course in a few years, and grow the drone business. Keep investing and maybe buy a house with Leila.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Pretty optimistic, honestly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to a nervous older miner?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Learn one new system and you'll be fine for years. I'd show them the remote cabin.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Anything that still worries you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not much for me. Maybe for people who never want to learn.

do: Take a **robotics course** in a few years, after the remote certificate.

fieldNote: He sees the slow AGI path as **good for him**.

steps.text: Take a robotics course in a few years

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because both of our incomes would be hit inside three years. What would help is income support for families during the switch and paid training for robot supervision. I'm the one who loves the new tech, and even I'd struggle if both our jobs went inside three years.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask about partners. Most people think about their own job, but the household is where it really hits.

He uses **AI every day** and runs a small drone hobby business.
His worry comes mostly from **Leila's exposure** to AI.

biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because both his and Leila's incomes would be hit within three years.
